title: Vessantara's giving
hookLine: the prince who gave past every limit, and the old question about him.
tomorrow: what can you give in a single day that costs no money at all?

lines: THE JACKET, SURE. THE CAR, NO.
cards: Most people keep a quiet limit on giving. The old jacket, sure. The car, no.

So what would you give away if it cost you nearly everything? Tradition places one prince, Vessantara, in the Buddha's last life before the one in which he woke up, and his story is about giving past every limit.
A gentle word for parents: in this story he gives away even his own children, and it's a hard one to hear.

teach.b: Vessantara is a prince who can't say no to anyone who asks. He gives the kingdom's precious white elephant to envoys from a land in drought, and his own people, furious, send him into exile.
On the road out he gives away his chariot and his horses.
In the forest, with his wife Maddi and their two children, a greedy old man comes asking for the children as servants, and Vessantara gives them. Then a stranger asks for Maddi.

She's given too, and the stranger turns out to be Sakka, king of the gods, who hands her straight back. In the end the children are ransomed by their grandfather, and the family comes home. Here's what's worth noticing.
Buddhists didn't pretend this was easy.

teach.h: KING MILINDA ASKS: WAS IT RIGHT?
teach.b: In the Questions of King Milinda, the king asks the monk Nagasena whether giving away a wife and children was right, and Nagasena has to work to answer. The question sits inside the tradition's own books.
What the story teaches, under all that, is today's line: generosity costs. The giving it praises isn't spare change.

how: The Vessantara Jataka is retold and performed in Theravada lands, sometimes recited in full at a temple festival; monks and teachers also discuss its hard parts, as the Questions of King Milinda does.

games.q: your nine-year-old hears the story and asks, "why would a dad give his kids away?" what's an honest answer from the lesson?
o: it shows good people should give everything, even family.
it's a hard story; even old Buddhist books ask if it was right.
it's about servants, and things were just different back then.
games.why: the story praises giving past every limit, and the tradition also asks the hard question out loud, in the Questions of King Milinda. the family comes home in the end.

practice: Hold, or picture, one thing you value that someone else could really use. Notice the pull to keep it, and stay with that pull without obeying it or fighting it. Then ask yourself, quietly: could I give this gladly?

wordCard.voice: Vessantara's giving: the prince who gave past every limit, in the last of the long Jataka tales. Praised, and argued over.
